content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published this document in 2018, granting permission for non-commercial use, adaptation, and redistribution of its content, provided proper citation is given. The WHO logo cannot be used, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, a disclaimer must be included stating that the translation was not produced by WHO and that the original English version remains the authoritative edition. Disputes regarding the license are to be mediated under the rules of the World Intellectual Property Organization. The document outlines specifications for pesticide application equipment used in vector control, aiming to assist public health authorities in selecting high-quality equipment. This second edition builds on the 2010 revised edition and includes specifications for equipment used in larvicide application and additional adulticide equipment. Manufacturers are required to provide warranties against manufacturing defects, after-sales service, and compliance with national or international standards. WHO no longer tests pesticide application equipment for compliance with its specifications. National programs or manufacturers seeking evaluation must arrange testing with WHO-approved laboratories. Feedback on equipment performance is encouraged to validate compliance with WHO specifications. Manufacturers must supply user manuals in relevant languages, provide technical support, and assist in training local vector control staff on proper equipment use, maintenance, and storage. The document also describes various pesticide application techniques for vector control, including indoor residual spraying, space spraying, larval control, and barrier treatments. Indoor residual spraying involves applying insecticide to interior wall surfaces to control mosquitoes that rest indoors. Space treatments target flying adult insects with small droplets that remain airborne, using equipment such as thermal foggers or cold foggers. Larval control involves treating aquatic habitats with insecticides in various formulations, such as sprays, granules, or tablets, using equipment like compression sprayers or mist blowers. Barrier treatments involve spraying vegetation near homes with residual insecticides to kill resting mosquitoes. The guidelines emphasize the importance of using corrosion-resistant materials in equipment construction, ensuring operator safety, and maintaining operational performance. Equipment must be designed to prevent pesticide leakage and meet weight limits specified by national health and safety regulations. Testing procedures for equipment are outlined, and manufacturers are expected to provide essential spare parts and technical support.
